enrichment.short_title: Duomatic principle validates shareholders' agreement capital call despite inquorate board
key_facts: Monecor and Euro Brokers were equal shareholders in joint venture EBFL under a 1998 Shareholders' Agreement containing a capital call and declining-shareholder buy-out mechanism in clause 11(2).

In October 2000 EBFL had no B directors appointed by Monecor, so its board was inquorate when Finance Director Mr Pask emailed a £250,000 capital call; Monecor paid £100,000 but failed to pay the remaining £150,000 by the agreed deadline.
Euro Brokers exercised the clause 11(2) option to acquire Monecor's shares and obtained specific performance from Deputy High Court Judge Kosmin QC.
Monecor appealed on grounds that no valid board-issued capital call had been made, that the call exceeded FSA minimum regulatory capital, and that Euro Brokers had acted unconscionably.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a Deputy High Court Judge's order granting specific performance of a share transfer obligation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; specific performance affirmed, stay lifted, leave to appeal to the House of Lords refused, and Monecor ordered to pay Euro Brokers' appeal costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where all shareholders in a company unanimously assent to treat an informal funding notice as a capital call under a shareholders' agreement, the Duomatic principle applies even though the agreement requires notice from a properly constituted board; members may by conduct waive formal procedural requirements in a contract regulating their relationship, and a buffer above minimum regulatory capital may fall within a capital adequacy call.
legal_issues: Whether a capital call under clause 11(2) required a notice issued by a quorate board of EBFL
Whether the Duomatic principle applies to contractual procedural requirements in a shareholders' agreement
Whether the call was limited to FSA minimum regulatory capital or could include an agreed buffer
Whether Monecor waived procedural defects or was estopped from challenging the call
Whether the court should refuse specific performance for unconscionable conduct

enrichment.short_title: Father-son boundary dispute turns on 1976 conveyance measurements over plan
key_facts: Alan Druce and his father Roger disputed ownership of plot A of Parsonage Meadow at Frieth Hill, Henley-on-Thames, a valuable building plot adjoining Alan's house Hillside.
Edwin Druce conveyed land to Alan in September 1976 with a parcels clause describing a 90-foot frontage, while the annexed plan was ambiguous as to whether plots A and B or only plot B were included.
Earlier 1983 proceedings between Edwin, Roger and Alan were settled by a Tomlin order transferring Edwin's assets to Roger, but the judge held it did not acknowledge Alan's title to plot A.
Alan also relied on estoppel by representation arising from joint litigation conduct and 1992 solicitor correspondence about a right of way.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal with limited permission from Robert Englehart QC's order determining a boundary dispute.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the judge was held correct that the 1976 conveyance conveyed only a 90-foot frontage and that neither the Tomlin order nor estoppel by representation gave Alan title to plot A.
enrichment.ratio: Where a conveyance uses combined wording that the plan is 'for the purpose of identification only' and 'more particularly delineated', the verbal description in the parcels clause ordinarily prevails over the plan; extrinsic evidence such as fencing, a 1975 letter agreement, and physical features supported a 90-foot frontage, and a Tomlin order settling litigation between grandfather and father did not resolve title between father and son.
legal_issues: Construction of the 20 September 1976 conveyance as to whether plot A was included
Effect of the 1 July 1991 Tomlin order on ownership of plots A and H
Whether Roger was estopped by representation from denying Alan owned plot A
Admissibility and weight of extrinsic evidence where plan and parcels clause are ambiguous

enrichment.short_title: Advertisement hoarding appeals dismissed after inspector applied amenity test

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning Act 1990
provisions: section 54A (development plan duty — noted as inapplicable to advertisements)

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Control of Advertisements) Regulations 1992
provisions: Regulation 4(1) (control in interests of amenity and public safety)

key_facts: JC Decaux Ltd appealed to an inspector against Leeds City Council refusals of express consent for illuminated display panels on Whitehall Road, Leeds.

The council relied on Policy BD12 of the Unitary Development Plan and visual amenity; the claimant argued BD12 was over-prescriptive and cited comparable approved sites and PPG19 consistency requirements.
The inspector dismissed both appeals, finding visual clutter at an attractive rebuilt railway bridge gateway despite similarities with other major-route sites.
The claimant challenged the decision letter under section 288 on five grounds including materiality of BD12, adequacy of reasons, fairness, consistency, and Wednesbury unreasonableness.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application under section 288 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to quash an inspector's advertisement consent appeal decisions.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed on all grounds; claimant ordered to pay the first defendant's costs summarily assessed at £5,331.
enrichment.ratio: Development plan policies concerned with amenity may be material under Regulation 4 of the Advertisements Regulations provided each proposal is assessed on its particular merits in the interests of amenity; an inspector's reference to 'other material considerations' does not invalidate a decision if reasoning in fact turns on amenity alone, and describing a prominent route as a city 'gateway' based on site inspection is not a new issue requiring further hearing.
legal_issues: Whether Policy BD12 was an unlawful or immaterial consideration under the Advertisements Regulations
Whether the inspector adequately addressed over-prescriptiveness and consistency arguments
Whether describing the site as a gateway raised a new unaddressed issue
Whether reasons on consistency with comparable sites were adequate
Whether the inspector's visual amenity conclusion was Wednesbury unreasonable or disproportionate

enrichment.short_title: Police depression from promotion failure held not injury received in execution of duty

statutes_considered.title: Police Pensions Regulations 1987
provisions: Regulation A11 (injury received in execution of duty)

key_facts: Inspector Trevor Clinch of Dorset Police was retired on ill-health grounds in December 2000 with depression after repeated failure to obtain promotion, including rejection for Chief Inspector Operations Manager at Poole in March 2000.

The Police Authority refused his injury-on-duty award claim without referring medical questions to a practitioner under Regulation H1, holding the psychiatric condition was not received in execution of duty.
The Crown Court dismissed his Regulation H5 appeal, relying on R v Stunt v Mallett, and the case was stated to the High Court.
McCombe J held the Authority must refer H1 questions once considering an injury pension claim, but depression caused by promotion disappointment was not an injury in execution of duty.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from the Crown Court to the High Court on Police Pensions Regulations 1987 questions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Crown Court held correct that the claim could not succeed and need not be referred to a medical practitioner where bound to fail, though on H1 construction a reference would otherwise be required.
enrichment.ratio: Regulation H1(2) of the Police Pensions Regulations 1987 requires reference to a medical practitioner once a police authority considers an injury pension claim, but a Crown Court may dismiss an appeal without referral where the claim is bound to fail; psychiatric injury caused by disappointment at failure to obtain promotion arises from being a police officer rather than from execution of duty and falls outside the Stunt line of authority.
legal_issues: Whether a police authority may decide 'injury in execution of duty' without medical reference under Regulation H1
Construction of 'considering whether to grant an injury pension' in Regulation H1(2)
Whether psychiatric illness from promotion failure is an injury received in execution of duty
Application of R v Stunt v Mallett and Kellam to stress-related police pension claims

enrichment.short_title: Drink-drive special reasons quashed for failing objective emergency test
key_facts: Manjit Singh Ubhi pleaded guilty to driving with excess alcohol (61 micrograms per 100ml breath) on 4 June 2002.
After his sister fell in a student hall bathroom, he drove her toward hospital when delegated attempts to obtain an ambulance and taxi failed; police stopped the car and an ambulance was called.
Telford justices found special reasons not to disqualify, citing duress of circumstances, a genuine medical emergency, delegated enquiries, and police confirmation of distress.
The sister was discharged within about an hour with advice and painkillers; the DPP appealed by case stated.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from magistrates to the High Court against a finding of special reasons not to disqualify for drink-driving.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; justices' decision quashed and case remitted to a differently constituted bench; respondent ordered to pay appellant's costs subject to detailed assessment.
enrichment.ratio: Special reasons not to disqualify a drink-driver require objective assessment under Taylor v Rajan of the gravity of the emergency and whether a sober reasonable person would have driven rather than made further enquiries; a finding of 'duress of circumstances' is inappropriate where the defendant pleaded guilty, and reliance on delegated failed attempts to summon help without finding what a reasonable person would have done vitiates the decision.
legal_issues: Whether justices applied the correct objective test for special reasons
Whether duress of circumstances can coexist with a guilty plea and special reasons
Whether delegation of enquiries to another person satisfied the requirement to explore alternatives
Whether the post-arrest seriousness of the sister's condition undermined the emergency finding

enrichment.short_title: Robbery conviction quashed for street identification breach of PACE Code D
key_facts: Minor appellant K was convicted at Grays Magistrates' Court of robbery after a group demanded money and a mobile phone from the victim in November 2001.
Police pulled K to a car window for street identification by the victim without holding a Code D identification parade, despite K disputing involvement and protesting innocence.
An earlier trial was discontinued after dock identifications; a further witness statement was taken before retrial but the district judge refused a stay for abuse of process.
The district judge treated participation as the main issue but Henriques J held identification was live and that D.2.17 and mandatory D.2.3 requirements under Forbes were breached.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Grays Magistrates' Court to the High Court against robbery conviction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; conviction quashed because identification evidence should have been excluded under section 78; no order for recovery of defence costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where a suspect disputes identification after a street confrontation in breach of PACE Code D paragraph D.2.17, an identification procedure under D.2.3 is mandatory unless D.2.15 applies; following Forbes, prior unequivocal identification does not displace that duty, and evidence obtained by directing a witness to the suspect at a police car should be excluded under section 78 as unfair.
legal_issues: Whether proceedings should be stayed after dock identifications and a further witness statement
Whether failure to hold an identification parade breached Code D.2.3
Whether street identification breached Code D.2.17
Whether the district judge should have excluded identification evidence under section 78

enrichment.short_title: Gatwick Airport HSWA prosecution remitted after magistrate rejected inference of risk

statutes_considered.title: Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974
provisions: section 33(1)(a) (offence for failure to discharge duty)

key_facts: Passenger Urwashi Patel suffered a degloving finger injury on 9 May 2000 while being driven in an invalid buggy through a doorway at Gatwick North Terminal.
A fire door came off its magnetic catch and closed as she put her hand out; a protruding screw on the push plate caught her ring.
Health and safety inspector Mr Smith prosecuted Gatwick Airport Ltd for breaching section 3(1); the district judge upheld no case to answer for lack of evidence of exposure to risk.
Prior maintenance records showed recurring magnetic catch faults on the door, though reasonable practicability was not reached at that stage.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Brighton Magistrates' Court after submission of no case to answer at close of prosecution case.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; case remitted to the district judge; respondent ordered to pay appellant's costs of £12,325.83.
enrichment.ratio: In a section 3 HSWA prosecution the Crown must prove exposure to risk to health and safety, which may be established by irresistible inference from primary facts even without res ipsa loquitur; where witness evidence showed a fire door closing when it should have remained open and a protruding screw caused immediate injury, a magistrate erred in treating causation and risk as mere assumption.
legal_issues: Whether prosecution evidence established exposure to risk without proof of exact cause
Whether inferences from primary facts could prove causation and risk in a criminal health and safety case
Whether res ipsa loquitur applied
Whether reasonable practicability had to be proved before the section 40 burden arose

enrichment.short_title: Prison death inquest neglect directions flawed but fresh inquest refused

statutes_considered.title: Human Rights Act 1998
provisions: Article 2 ECHR (impact on inquest verdict scope)

key_facts: Darren Davies, 23, died of dehydration at HM Prison Birmingham on 5 March 2001 while withdrawing from heroin; the inquest jury returned accidental death.
He missed detoxification doses after a misplaced treatment card and received inadequate follow-up despite repeated cell buzzer calls, vomiting, and spasms over the weekend before collapse.
Independent prison doctor Dr Ralli criticised follow-up failures and Nurse Spencer's assessment; the coroner excluded parts of his report and misdirected on neglect.
The claimant mother sought judicial review alleging misdirection on neglect, system failure, and exclusion of expert evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a deputy coroner's summing-up following an inquest into a death in prison custody.
enrichment.outcome: Coroner misdirected on individual and system neglect, but verdict not quashed and no fresh inquest ordered because a full inquiry had occurred and the coroner had already recommended systemic improvements.
enrichment.ratio: A coroner's neglect direction must explain that gross failure may be found even where a clinician exercised judgment, and after Amin and Middleton a jury may consider system neglect to meet Article 2 objectives; however relief by way of fresh inquest is discretionary and may be refused where evidence was fully explored and recommendations already made to the prison.
legal_issues: Meaning of neglect following Jamieson and Amin and Middleton
Whether Nurse Spencer's clinical judgment precluded a neglect verdict
Whether system defects in drug-withdrawal follow-up should have been left to the jury
Whether exclusion of parts of Dr Ralli's evidence vitiated the inquest
Appropriate remedy where summing-up was deficient but inquiry was comprehensive

enrichment.short_title: Underground station assault conviction upheld despite honest witness discrepancy

statutes_considered.title: Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984
provisions: section 78 (exclusion of unfair evidence — raised but not pursued on appeal)

key_facts: Mr Forde was convicted of common assault on London Underground employee Maureen Quinn at Green Park station on 4 July 2001 after following her to a mess room.

Quinn said Forde barged her into the doorframe with his shoulder as she opened the mess room door; independent witness Johnson saw her open the door and Forde put his foot in the door but saw no physical contact.
The Crown Court rejected a section 78 application to exclude Quinn's evidence over late disclosure of Johnson; Forde was conditionally discharged for 12 months.
On case stated appeal, Moses J held the court was entitled to be sure of Quinn's account despite Johnson's evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from the Crown Court to the High Court against conviction for common assault.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Crown Court entitled to convict where sure of the complainant's evidence notwithstanding an honest independent witness who did not see contact.
enrichment.ratio: Where two honest witnesses give apparently inconsistent accounts of a brief incident, a fact-finding court may convict if sure the complainant tells the truth; imperfect rationalisation of how an independent witness missed part of the incident does not vitiate a conviction grounded on credibility findings meeting the criminal standard.
legal_issues: Whether Crown Court findings reconciling Quinn and Johnson were open on the evidence
Whether late prosecution disclosure of Johnson required exclusion under section 78 or a stay
Whether finding Johnson unlikely to have seen the assault reflected improper burden of proof

enrichment.short_title: Extended-sentence recall engages Article 5 but Sim's continued detention upheld

statutes_considered.title: Crime and Disorder Act 1998
provisions: section 58 (extended sentence — now mirrored in PCC(S)A 2000 s 85)

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice Act 1991
provisions: section 44A (Parole Board review and release test)

key_facts: Mr Sim received an extended sentence in February 2000 for indecent assault and indecency with a child: 30 months custody plus five years' extended licence.
He was released on licence in January 2001 but recalled in July 2001 after alcohol breaches, hostel aggression, and a later-withdrawn indecent exposure allegation.
The Parole Board refused release in April 2002, finding high risk of further sexual or violent offending and failed supervision in the community.
He sought judicial review challenging Article 5 applicability, the recall test, section 44A presumption of detention, and reliance on disputed hearsay.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Parole Board's decision refusing release after recall during an extended licence period.
enrichment.outcome: Claim largely failed on the facts; declarations made that Article 5 applies to extended-licence recall and section 44A must be read compatibly so release is required unless the Board is positively satisfied confinement is necessary; leave to appeal granted.
enrichment.ratio: Recall detention during the extended licence period engages Article 5 and must pursue the sentencing judge's preventive objectives with periodic review; section 44A is incompatible if read as presuming continued detention unless the prisoner proves otherwise and must be construed under section 3 HRA so the Parole Board releases unless positively satisfied confinement is necessary, but continuing detention is lawful where supervision has broken down and there is a real risk of further sexual or violent offending within the extended sentence's scope.
legal_issues: Whether Article 5 applies to detention following recall during extended licence
Whether the legislative recall scheme infringes Article 5.1 or 5.4
Correct test for Parole Board release after extended-sentence recall
Whether risk must be of serious harm or high likelihood
Construction of section 44A presumption of detention
Fairness of relying on disputed hearsay without oral evidence
